title: Private DNS + Reverse-Proxy Patterns for Regulated POC
content:
Purpose
This note captures a lightweight, testable pattern for customers in regulated industries who require: private DNS resolution, auditable outbound egress through a controlled reverse-proxy, and minimal attack surface on inference hosts. Goal is a POC that proves: deterministic DNS handoff, TLS inspection/termination at a controlled egress proxy, preservation of per-tenant routing and logs, and low operational complexity for the customer.

Context / problem statement
- Customer: finance SaaS (simulated PII workloads). They want private-hosted Redwood Private in their VPC with strong egress controls.
- Constraints: no direct internet access from model hosts, no NAT gateway (security policy prefers NATless), must route all outbound requests through an auditable proxy, split-horizon DNS where internal names resolve to internal endpoints, and public model downloads must be mediated and logged.
- Success criteria for POC: 1) DNS requests for model-serving domains resolve to internal proxy endpoints, 2) outbound model downloads succeed via proxy with logged request/response hashes, 3) inference latency within SLA-hit budget (< 100ms additional tail from proxy for small prompts), 4) clear operational runbook.

Design principles
- Minimize network primitives customer must change: prefer interface endpoints (PrivateLink) and conditional DNS over heavy route table surgery.
- Keep inference hosts strictly private (no public IPs).
- Single egress chokepoint (reverse-proxy) that can perform TLS termination or TLS passthrough depending on customer policy.
- Prefer TLS-over-DNS / DOH or DoT for resolver hops when possible to avoid leaking FQDNs to upstream resolvers.
- Auditing and non-repudiation: store request metadata, checksum of model binaries, and proxy logs in immutable storage (S3 with write-only bucket policy + KMS).

High-level topology (textual)
- VPC-A: private-subnet (inference hosts), mgmt-subnet (ops), proxy-subnet (reverse-proxies / egress-gw), resolver-subnet (route 53 inbound/forwarder).
- Interface Endpoint(s): com.amazonaws.s3 (for model artifact fetch gating if using S3-hosted artifacts), com.custom.redwood.private-controlplane (PrivateLink to Redwood control plane for model registry calls)
- Reverse-proxy (ephemeral ASG) in proxy-subnet with SG allowing outbound 443 only to whitelisted upstreams. Ingress from private-subnet via SG allow on 8443 (mutual TLS) or 3128 (http proxy).

Two recommended modes (customer selects):
1) TLS-termination proxy (recommended for deep inspection/compliance)
   - Proxy terminates TLS, validates client mTLS certs from inference hosts, performs request/response logging, optionally modifies headers (inject tenant-id).
   - Downstream connection to upstream can be TLS to public endpoint or to internal PrivateLink endpoint.
   - Pros: full visibility, easier content checks and caching. Cons: more crypto work and cert management, potential TLS break requirements.

2) TLS-passthrough proxy (recommended where MITM is disallowed)
   - Proxy routes raw TLS (SNI-based) to upstream via CONNECT or L4 proxy. Logging limited to metadata (SNI, IP, bytes).
   - Use if regulatory rules prevent decrypting packets.
   - Pros: simpler trust model, less cryptographic overhead. Cons: less content-level auditing.

DNS handoff and split-horizon
- Customer runs an internal resolver cluster in resolver-subnet (Unbound / CoreDNS) configured as authoritative for a subset of zones used by Redwood in private deployments (e.g., *.redwood-private.local).
- Option A: Conditional forwarder for public hostnames used by model registries -> forward to a local proxy IP (the proxy acts as DNS sink and answers with 127.0.0.1-like internal resolution or CNAME to internal LB). This prevents direct egress for artifact downloads and ensures artifact fetches go via proxy.
- Option B: Route53 Resolver inbound endpoints + outbound rules (AWS example) where rules forward matching domains (model-registry.example.com, artifacts.example.com) to the proxy or to a resolver that returns PrivateLink IPs. Use DoT/DoH to upstream if policy requires encrypted queries.
- Critical: ensure systemd/resolv.conf on inference hosts points to resolver-subnet IPs and that DHCP options in the VPC do not leak external DNS.

Endpoints and service connectivity
- Use Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) where Redwood offers control-plane or artifact services inside the customer network. This provides stable private IPs and avoids public egress for control-plane traffic.
- Use Gateway Endpoints only for cloud-managed storage (S3) if artifact storage is used and customer allows direct S3 access. If not allowed, gate S3 via proxy.
- For hybrid on-prem customers: leverage equivalent on-prem DNS conditional forwarding to the VPC resolver or a tunnel to the proxy cluster (WireGuard/IPSec) with strict source IP translation so logs show originating tenant.

Security controls
- Security Groups: inference hosts allow only outbound to proxy-subnet on ports defined (8443, 3128). Proxy SG allows outbound only to whitelisted upstream IPs or PrivateLink endpoints.
- NACLs: optional additional egress block for 0.0.0.0/0 except proxy.
- IAM: proxy has role for logging to S3/KMS only; inference hosts do not have direct S3 get permissions unless explicitly required and logged.
- mTLS: recommended between inference hosts and proxy to prevent host spoofing. TLS context: short-lived certs issued by customer CA + cert rotation automation.
- WAF: if terminating TLS at proxy, optionally run WAF rules for known bad patterns. Avoid broad rules that could mutate model payloads.

Operational runbook (POC scope)
- Step 0: baseline metrics collection (latency, egress rate, artifact download success) on a non-blocking sample.
- Step 1: Deploy resolver cluster and adjust DHCP/resolv.conf for a single dev host. Confirm internal names resolve to resolver.
- Step 2: Stand up proxy in proxy-subnet with minimal config (TLS passthrough). Confirm inference host can reach model registry via proxy.
- Step 3: Toggle to TLS-termination mode on proxy for a limited tenant and verify artifact checksum logging and header injection.
- Step 4: Test failure cases: proxy down, proxy slow, DNS misresolve. Validate fallback paths (cannot default to direct egress).
- Step 5: Load test artifact downloads (100s of simultaneous small files and a few large model files) and measure tail latency and proxy CPU/RAM.
- Step 6: Capture logs, ship to immutable S3 prefix, and run verification script to cross-check checksums.

Checklist for POC run
- [ ] Resolver cluster deployed and resolv.conf pinned on test hosts
- [ ] Interface endpoints created for Redwood control plane
- [ ] Proxy autoscaling group + health checks in place
- [ ] Mutual TLS certs minted and installed (or proof for passthrough mode)
- [ ] Logging to S3 + lifecycle policy + KMS key created
- [ ] Test artifacts and known-checksum models uploaded to guarded storage
- [ ] Latency and throughput dashboards configured in Redwood Console

Testing matrix (recommended)
- DNS resolution accuracy: 1000 random queries for critical FQDNs -> 100% internal answers
- Artifact fetch integrity: 50 downloads of each artifact size (small/medium/large) -> checksums match
- Proxy-induced latency: median / p95 / p99 before and after proxy insertion
- Fault injection: kill proxy nodes and confirm inference hosts fail closed (no direct internet egress)

Open questions / decisions for customer
- Does customer allow TLS termination for inspection? (policy dependent)
- Will customer accept PrivateLink for artifact hosting or require public artifact hosting with proxy gating?
- Expected throughput and concurrency for artifact downloads (this drives proxy sizing).
- Retention policy for audit logs and where they live (internal S3 vs external log archive).

Notes to SEs (lessons learned from prior POCs)
- Avoid complex route table edits; customers prefer resolver-based approaches.
- Cert automation is the most frequent blocker; have a scripted path for issuing short-lived certs using the customer CA or step-ca.
- Proxy caching of common artifact shards reduces cost and tail latency significantly — include cache warm-up in POC.
- Make the POC reversible: record exact DHCP options and resolver configs so we can revert to default quickly.

Appendix: quick commands (AWS-centric examples)
- Create Route53 Resolver rule to forward artifacts.example.com to resolver IP: aws route53resolver create-resolver-rule --creator-request-id poc-rule --domain-name artifacts.example.com --rule-type FORWARD --target-ips Ip=10.0.10.5
- Example curl via http proxy (passthrough): CURL_PROXY=10.0.20.10:3128 curl -v --resolve model-registry.example.com:443:10.0.20.10 https://model-registry.example.com/path/to/artifact

References / related tickets
- SE-4123: customer compliance intake
- Confluence: Private DNS Patterns (linked above)
- PR: private-deployments/#78 (sample proxy helm chart)

Next steps before demo
- Align with customer security (get explicit TLS-termination decision)
- Prepare cert automation runbook and brief infra team
- Schedule controlled demo with artifact download and checksum verification

Author: Ava Patel (SE)
Status: draft — feedback welcome, will iterate after internal review.
